previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a male with hepatitis C cirrhosis and portal hypertension, was admitted for melena and hematemesis following recent esophageal variceal banding. He presented with hypotension and evidence of upper GI bleeding, requiring transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells. An EGD revealed an esophageal ulcer and blood in the stomach, but no active bleeding; the previously placed variceal bands had dislodged. He was treated with octreotide, ceftriaxone (later switched to oral ciprofloxacin), and IV pantoprazole, which was transitioned to oral pantoprazole twice daily. Nadolol was held due to bradycardia, likely related to octreotide, but was restarted at discharge at half dose. His condition stabilized, hemoglobin remained steady, and he tolerated a diet advance. He was discharged home with instructions to complete a course of ciprofloxacin and sucralfate, continue high-dose PPI therapy, and follow up for repeat EGD and hepatology evaluation.

TACE procedure:
*** UNAPPROVED (PRELIMINARY) REPORT ***
INDICATION: ___ male with multifocal HCC. Transarterial
chemoembolization requested.
 
COMPARISON: MR of ___.
 
PHYSICIANS: Dr. ___ (attending, present and supervising 
throughout)
and Dr. ___ (fellow).
 
ANESTHESIA/MEDICATIONS: Moderate sedation was provided by 
administering
divided doses of fentanyl (75 mcg) and Versed (1.5 mg) 
throughout the total
intraservice time of 1 hour and 35 minutes during which the 
patient's
hemodynamic parameters were monitored continuously by an 
independent radiology
nurse. In addition, the patient received 30 mg IV Toradol, 20 mL
intra-arterial 1% lidocaine and 0.25 mg of Dilaudid. 
Chemoembolization
consisted of 6 mg of doxorubicin and 20 mL of lipiodol.
 
FLUOROSCOPY: 655 mGy, 29 minutes.
 
CONTRAST: 108 mL Optiray.
 
PROCEDURES:
1. Right CFA access with a micropuncture needle.
2. Common hepatic arteriogram and rotational cone-beam CT.
3. Transarterial chemoembolization of the right hepatic artery
 
PROCEDURE DETAIL: After explanation of the risks, benefits and 
alternatives
to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained. The 
patient was
brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the 
imaging table. The
right groin was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. 
A
preprocedure timeout and huddle was performed as per ___ 
protocol.
 
Under palpatory, ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance, the right 
common
femoral artery was accessed with a micropuncture needle. A 0.018 
nitinol wire
was then advanced through the needle into the lower abdominal 
aorta. A small
skin incision was made over the needle and the needle was 
exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath. The inner cannula and dilator were removed 
with the
wire and a 0.035 ___ wire was advanced through the 
micropuncture sheath
into the lower abdominal aorta. The sheath was removed and a 5 
___
___ sheath was advanced over the wire. The sheath was then 
connected to
a continuous heparinized side arm flush.
 
Next, a C2 glide catheter was advanced over the ___ wire 
into the upper
abdominal aorta. The wire was removed and the celiac axis was 
selectively
cannulated, confirmed by a hand injection of contrast. With the 
assistance of
a Glidewire, the catheter was then advanced more distally into 
the common
hepatic artery. Digital subtraction angiogram with rotational 
DynaCT was
performed demonstrating conventional hepatic arterial anatomy. 
There are
several abnormal vessels arising from the proximal aspect of the 
right hepatic
artery supplying subtle areas of tumoral enhancement 
corresponding to findings
on MRI. The C2 catheter was advanced into the right hepatic 
artery and
chemoembolization was administered with tumor staining, 
particularly in the
segment VI/VII lesion. Next, a small amount Gelfoam was 
administered for
bland embolization to slow vascular flow. The patient received 5 
mL aliquots
of intra-arterial 1% lidocaine intermittently between 
administration of the
chemoembolization. The catheter was flushed and removed. The 
sheath was
removed and hemostasis was achieved with 15 minutes of manual 
compression.
 
The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate 
complication.
 
FINDINGS:
1. Conventional common hepatic arterial anatomy with multiple 
branches
arising from the right common hepatic artery and supplying the 
dominant tumor
as well as smaller tumors.
2. Slowed flow to the dominant lesion and other lesions after 
administration
of chemoembolization and bland embolization material.
 
IMPRESSION: Uncomplicated transarterial chemoembolization to the 
RHA.
Findings and recommendations discussed with Dr. ___ at 1 
p.m. on
___.

CT abdomen post TACE
TECHNIQUE:  CT of the abdomen without IV contrast.
 
FINDINGS:  Lung bases are clear.  There is no Lipiodol 
distribution in the
lung bases.
 
ABDOMEN:  Within the liver, the dominant tumor in segment VI/VII 
has dense
Lipiodol uptake as does the remainder of the right lobe of the 
liver.  Air
noted within the liver (3, 17 and 3, 26), likely a result of 
recent
procedure.There is no non-targeted Lipiodol uptake noted.  The 
gallbladder
contains dense stones.
 
Non-contrast appearance of the pancreas and stomach are 
unremarkable.  The
spleen is enlarged at 18 cm.  The renal vasculature contain 
scattered
calcifications as does the abdominal aorta.  There are also tiny 
punctate
calcifications in bilateral kidneys representing very small 
stones,
non-obstructing.  A renal cyst is noted all through the right 
kidney.
 
The mesentery is in general misty with a small amount of fluid, 
likely ascites
in both paracolic gutters.  There is a recanalized umbilical 
vein along with
prominent varices elsewhere throughout the abdomen including 
gastric and
esophageal.  
 
IMPRESSION:
1.  Good Lipiodol uptake within the dominant liver lesion as 
well as in the
remainder of the right lobe of the liver.  No non-target 
embolization
identified.
2.  Splenomegaly, varices, tiny renal non-obstructing renal 
stones and
cholelithiasis.
